opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to a shift in where we are with AI. For a long time, the bottleneck was methods: we didn't have models that could do much, so the field rightly focused on inventing better architectures and training techniques, and benchmarks were mostly a way to measure that progress. Whether the benchmark task was actually useful didn't matter much, because any improvement on something hard like ImageNet or a reading comprehension dataset signaled a better method.

Now we have a pretty general recipe: large-scale pretraining, plus reasoning and reinforcement learning, plus the ability to act through tools and environments. That recipe tends to crush benchmarks very quickly. So if you keep designing tasks in the old way, as abstract puzzles or isolated exam questions, you get this strange situation where models score superhumanly on many benchmarks, yet the economic or practical impact in the real world doesn't move proportionally. There's a gap between the scores and the utility.

To me, that gap means our evaluations are measuring the wrong things. Real-world work has properties most benchmarks ignore. It's long-horizon, not one-shot. It involves interacting with people, so the agent has to clarify intent and handle ambiguity. It happens in messy environments with real tools, real codebases, real websites. And success is often about reliability: does it work consistently, not just once out of many tries. When we built things like WebShop, SWE-bench, or tau-bench, the idea was to bring some of that reality into evaluation, such as a user in the loop, actual repositories, or pass-at-k-style consistency.

So the question becomes: what should an agent actually be able to do that creates value for someone? If you define the task around that, then optimizing for the benchmark more directly translates into optimizing for usefulness. In a way, evaluation becomes the thing that drives research, because whoever defines the right problem shapes what everyone builds toward. In this second phase of AI, I think defining the problem well may matter as much as, or more than, solving it.

r001.rationale: The response describes broadly effective AI methods and argues that better task definitions can steer research toward usefulness, but it does not say that a well-designed reward makes a task close to solvable.

r002.rationale: The response cites ambiguity, messy environments, and reliability as challenges, but it does not identify the absence of a standard reward function as a reason real-world tasks are difficult.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the simplest way to put it is: the thing we are optimizing for should be the thing we actually want. For a long time in AI, and especially in agents, that hasn't been the case. We've been optimizing for benchmarks that are easy to build and easy to score, not for tasks that matter to anyone.

Let me back up a bit. In my view, the history of AI research has been a kind of loop between methods and tasks. You come up with a new training method or architecture, and then you need a task to show it works. For most of the field's history, the method side was the bottleneck, so it made sense that tasks were designed for convenience. You pick something like a game, or a question-answering dataset, where the environment is cheap and the reward is clean. ImageNet, Atari, these were great because they let the method people iterate fast.

But I think we're now at a point where the bottleneck has flipped. The methods, meaning pretraining plus reinforcement learning, actually work surprisingly generally. If you give the model a reasonable environment with a reasonable reward signal, it will learn. So the hard, high-leverage question is no longer "how do I train it," it's "what do I train it on, and how do I know it's good." That's a task design and evaluation question. And once that's the bottleneck, convenience is no longer a good enough reason to pick a task.

There's also a very concrete failure mode I've seen, which is that an agent can look superhuman on a benchmark and still be basically useless. When I worked on things like WebShop or SWE-bench, one thing that became clear is that the gap between "solves the benchmark" and "a real person would trust this with their work" is huge. Benchmarks are usually stateless, you reset every episode, the task is fully specified, and the evaluation is pass or fail on a fixed ground truth. Real work is almost the opposite. Tasks are underspecified. The user changes their mind. You have to interact with people, not just with tools. You have to remember what happened last week. You might have to do something for days. None of that shows up in a one-shot accuracy number. So if your evaluation ignores all of it, you can climb to ninety-something percent and have learned nothing about whether the agent is useful.

The other point is about what "utility" even means. I think the field tends to treat evaluation as an afterthought: build the model, then find a number. But I'd argue evaluation is where you encode your values. If you decide the metric is pass@1 on a set of GitHub issues, you are implicitly saying that solving isolated, well-defined coding problems is what matters. If instead you measure things like how much of a developer's week an agent can take over, or whether a user comes back and uses it again, you're encoding a very different, and in my opinion more honest, objective. And models will go where the metric points. They are extremely good at that. So the metric had better point somewhere we want to end up.

I also think there's a practical argument for researchers, not just for products. Real-world tasks are a much richer source of signal. If you build an environment grounded in something people actually do, you automatically get diversity, long horizons, ambiguity, and recovery from errors, because reality has all of that for free. You don't have to artificially inject difficulty. And when something fails, the failure tells you something true about the world rather than about an artifact of your benchmark design. That's a much better flywheel.

Finally, and maybe this is the part I care about most, I think it's about the next phase of AI. The first phase was mostly about proving that intelligence can be built. We've largely done that; these systems can reason and use tools and pass very hard exams. The question now is whether that intelligence turns into something that changes how people live and work, which is actually what the whole project was supposed to be about. That transition doesn't happen by making benchmarks harder in a vacuum. It happens by picking tasks where success means someone's job got easier, or something got discovered, or a product got built. So when I say agent research should focus more on real-world value, I don't mean it as a product slogan. I mean it as a research strategy: the problems that are worth solving are also the ones that will teach us the most, and we've reached the point where we can afford to work on them directly.

r001.rationale: The response says current methods work generally and that, given a reasonable environment and reward signal, the model will learn.

r002.rationale: It describes real-world tasks as underspecified and complex, but does not identify the lack of a standard reward function as a reason they are difficult to solve.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is: if an agent succeeds at a task, what does that success actually mean for someone? A benchmark score can tell us that a system is getting better at a particular test, but it doesn’t automatically tell us that the system is useful.

In the real world, people care about whether the work gets done, how much time and money it takes, and how often they need to intervene. An agent might complete an impressive sequence of actions, but if checking and correcting its output takes longer than doing the task yourself, its practical value is limited. So those costs should be part of the evaluation, rather than something we consider afterward.

This also changes task design. Instead of starting with what is easy to score, we should start with a real need and ask what successful completion would look like. Real tasks often involve ambiguity, incomplete information, and situations where asking a question is better than continuing autonomously. We want evaluations that reward that judgment.

Research benchmarks are still useful. But ultimately, we need a connection between progress on those benchmarks and progress in helping people. Otherwise, we risk making agents better at passing tests without making them better at doing useful work.

r001.rationale: The response discusses practical evaluation and task design but does not claim that existing general solution methods make tasks with well-designed rewards nearly solvable.

r002.rationale: It mentions ambiguity and incomplete information as real-world challenges, but does not identify the lack of a standard reward function as a reason tasks are difficult to solve.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is: if an agent does well on a task, what does that actually mean for people? Does it save someone time, solve a problem they care about, or let them do something they couldn’t do before? If we can’t connect the score to those outcomes, it’s hard to know whether we’re making meaningful progress.

It’s relatively easy to design tasks that are convenient to evaluate: the environment is clean, the objective is explicit, and there’s one correct answer. But real work often involves figuring out what the user wants, finding missing information, and checking whether the result actually meets their needs. Those are part of the agent’s job, too.

So I think we should work backward from useful outcomes. Pick something people actually want done, then ask how reliably the agent can do it, how much human intervention it needs, and what it costs in time and money. A higher success rate isn’t necessarily useful if someone has to supervise every step.

That doesn’t mean every research task has to be a complete real-world application. Simplified tasks are valuable for understanding specific capabilities. But we need a connection between those capabilities and practical value. Otherwise, we risk getting very good at improving benchmark scores without knowing whether the agents are becoming more useful.

r001.rationale: The response discusses practical outcomes and evaluation, but does not say that well-designed rewards make tasks nearly solvable given existing general methods.

r002.rationale: It notes that real work involves unclear user needs and missing information, but does not identify the lack of a standard reward function as a reason real-world tasks are difficult to solve.
